Recall that statements of company policy, announced in handbooks or 
manuals for employees, have often been found to be incorporated in the 
terms of employment for personnel already in place, as wel as for new 
recruits. The "handbook" cases frequently permit employees to escape the 
rigors of the doctrine of at-will employment. See the discussion of Employee 
Handbooks, p. 94 above. In Berube v. Fashion Centre, Ltd., 771 P.2d 1033 
(Utah 1989), according to the lead opinion, the defendant 
Employer had 
"created and distributed a disciplinary action policy which was read and 
understood by the plaintiff," thereby limiting the grounds on which it could 
discharge her. The court reversed a judgment for the employer and ordered 
a retrial on the theory of an implied-in-fact contract. On these facts, was an 
offer any more evident than in Sayres?
